```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width=7,
  fig.height = 5
)
library(contcomp)
```

This package is designed to compare shapes of vessel or possibly other objects. It depends on the contour vectors
produced by [ISAAKiels shapAAR-package](https://github.com/ISAAKiel/shapAAR/) (hence the name). 
The contour vectors should ideally be in the format as illustrated by the files in ./inst/doc/. The contours in those 
files were produced with shapAAR (and a modification of the bulkIMGloop function that can be found there as a branch). 
I chose a larger image size and scaled the contours to 500px length, not 100px as proposed by ISAAKiel, to get a more detailed result. (Additionally I only used the left side of the drawings, so I could ignore the handles.)
Thumbs (./inst/img/) and txt-files (./inst/doc/) are included in this package, but not the original images, since I am unsure about the copyright. The sources are:  

* **Eilmann**: R. Eilmann, Frühe griechische Keramik im samischen Heraion, AM 58, 1933, 47--145  
* **Furtw**: A. Furtwängler, Heraion von Samos: Grabungen im Südtemenos 1977, I: Schicht- und Baubefund, Keramik, AM 95, 1980, 149--224  
* **Kopcke**: G. Kopcke, Heraion von Samos: Die Kampagnen 1961/1965 im Südtemenos, AM 83, 1968, 250--314  

The txt-files from one folder (*txtpath*) can be loaded into a single data frame with **load_shapaar_data()**:

```{r load_shapaar_contours}
txtpath = "../inst/doc/"
shapaardata_df <- load_shapaar_contours(txtpath)
knitr::kable(head(shapaardata_df))
```

In some cases, when the contours where not properly recognized or the automated rotation was slightly off, I encountered Inf-values in the Dataframe. The function **clean_bulkload_contour()** was designed to clean those values by replacing them with the one in the pre- or succeding row (depending on what's possible).

```{r clean_contour_df (remove infinites)}
any(is.infinite(rowSums(shapaardata_df)))
shapaardata_df <- clean_contour_df(shapaardata_df)
knitr::kable(head(shapaardata_df))
```


One of the purposes of this package was to automatically identify the 'areas' of a vessel, e.g. the rim, in order to later (automatically?) compare them with fragments. The **find_shinoto_index()**-function provides a data frame with such information, but currently it's only a start.

```{r find the points of interest (find_shinoto_index), warning=FALSE}
testcase_EilmannAbb4a <- find_shinoto_index(shapaardata_df[,1])
knitr::kable(head(testcase_EilmannAbb4a))
```

head_notation and foot_notation are still a 'work in progress', the index column relies on the 'points of interest' proposed by M. Shinoto (Shinoto 2008, Wege der Keramikklassifikation. Am Beispiel einer prähistorischen Irdenware aus Südjapan, see for example p. 250). Implementation is not yet done. 

There is a function that returns a plot illustrating the results. (Incidentally, the example below does not work very well. I provided another R-Script with a basic workflow to bulk-export those plots for all vessel from the initial data frame, and mostly they do work.)

```{r plot_shinoto_index}
plot_shinoto_index(testcase_EilmannAbb4a, "Eilmann 1933, Abb. 4a")
```





With another dataframe containing the polynomial models (although I am confident this should work with the original data frame as well), produced in this way: (Please also note that is is a transposed version.) Also, a second dataframe loaded from a .csv-file prepared beforehand with some information about the objects will come in handy to add information to the plots. 
```{r prepare for distance matrices and cluster analysis, warning=FALSE}
model_df <- data.frame(x=c(1:1000))
for (col in 1:ncol(shapaardata_df)) {
  wip <- find_shinoto_index(shapaardata_df[,col])
  model_df[,col] <- wip$modelcontour
  rm(wip)
}
model_df <- data.table::transpose(model_df)
rownames(model_df) <- gsub(".png.txt", "", colnames(shapaardata_df))

attrib_df <- NULL
attrib_df <- read.csv("../inst/doc/attrib.csv", sep=";", encoding = "UTF-8")
attrib_df$image <- paste("../inst/img/", attrib_df$file, "_thumb.png", sep = "") 
attrib_df$file <- gsub(".png", "", attrib_df$file)
colnames(attrib_df) <- c("label", "type", "attribute", "origin", "conservation", "thumb")
attrib_df$label <- as.factor(attrib_df$label)
attrib_df <- attrib_df[attrib_df$label %in% rownames(model_df),]
rownames(attrib_df) <- attrib_df$label
```



Three versions of a manual distance matrix (sadly not an object of class 'dist') can be produced (this may take some time):
```{r get the distance matrix, warning=FALSE}
#curve_dist <- get_curve_dist(model_df = model_df, type = "sd")
frechet_dist <- get_frechet_dist(model_df = model_df)
#procrustes_dist <- get_procrustes_dist(model_df = model_df)
```
**curve_dist()** was my own attempt at finding a way to quantify the (dis)similarity of two curves and uses either   

* the standard deviation of the 'difference curve' ('difference curve' = absolute values resulting from the subtraction of contour1 and contour2)  
* the sum of all values of said 'difference curve'  

SD seems to work better, but in the end both don't work as well as the [Frechet-Distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9chet_distance) (in this case from the package [SimilarityMeasures](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/SimilarityMeasures/versions/1.4/topics/Frechet)). I thought that the Procrustes-Distance might be worth a try, but am not happy with the results. 

I will only illustrate the results of the Frechet-Distance measure. There are two ways of visualizing the results, one being in a coordinate system with coordinates obtained via principal coordinates analysis (cmdscale()):

```{r principal coordinates analysis + plot, warning=FALSE}
frechet_coords <- as.data.frame(cmdscale(frechet_dist))
frechet_coords$label <- rownames(frechet_coords)
colnames(frechet_coords) <-  c("x", "y", "label")
frechet_coords <- merge(frechet_coords, attrib_df)
library(ggimage)
ggplot(data = frechet_coords, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_image(aes(image = thumb)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = type)) +
  coord_fixed()
```





This seems to seperate different types rather nicely. Maybe another dimension could be added to display the objects in a 3D-coordinate system, to differentiate a bit better.

contcomp provides some other functions to find similar and dissimilar vessels and visually compare them:

```{r find_max_dist + plot}
find_max_dist(frechet_dist)
plot_curve_diff(model_df, 'Kopcke_Kat57', 'Furtw_III-27')
```
```{r find_min_dist + plot}
find_min_dist(frechet_dist)
plot_curve_diff(model_df, 'Kopcke_Kat56', 'Eilmann_Abb4f')
```



The results might as well be displayed in a heatmap: 
```{r heatmap}
palette <- colorRampPalette(c('chartreuse4','white'))(256)
heatmap(frechet_dist, Rowv=F, scale='none', col=palette)
```

Or with a cluster dendrogram: 


```{r dendrogram}
library(ggdendro)
library(cluster)
clust <- diana(frechet_dist, metric = "euclidean")
dendr <- dendro_data(clust)
dendr$labels <- merge(dendr$labels, attrib_df)

ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data=segment(dendr), aes(x = x,
                                          y = y,
                                          xend = xend,
                                          yend = yend)) +
    geom_text(data=label(dendr), aes(x = x,
                                     y = y-3000,
                                     label = label,
                                     colour = type),
              size=3,
              hjust = 0) +
    geom_image(data=label(dendr), aes(x, y-3, image = thumb), size = .015) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_size_identity()
```
